etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English outward, from Old English ūtweard, equivalent to out +‎ -ward.

quote.citation: c. 1587–1588, [Christopher Marlowe], Tamburlaine the Great.  […]  The First Part […], 2nd edition, part 1, London:  […]  [R. Robinson for] Richard Iones, […], published 1592, →OCLC; reprinted as Tamburlaine the Great (A Scolar Press Facsimile), Menston, Yorkshire, London: Scolar Press, 1973, →ISBN, Act I, scene ii:
quote.text: Noble and milde this Perſean ſeemes to be,If outward habit Iudge the inward man.

definitions.definition: Tending to the exterior or outside.

quote.citation: 1700, [John] Dryden, “Sigismond and Guiscardo”, in Fables Ancient and Modern; […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The fire will force its outward way.

quote.citation: a. 1628 (date written), John Hayward, The Life, and Raigne of King Edward the Sixt, London:  […]  [Eliot’s Court Press, and J. Lichfield at Oxford?] for Iohn Partridge, […], published 1630, →OCLC:

definitions.definition: Towards the outside; away from the centre. [from 10th c.]

quote.citation: c. 1601–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Twelfe Night, or What You Will”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene i]:
quote.text: The wrong side may be turned outward.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Outwardly, in outer appearances; publicly. [14th–17th c.]

quote.citation: 1485, Sir Thomas Malory, “iij”, in Le Morte Darthur, book XVIII:
quote.text: ANd thenne the quene lete make a preuy dyner in london vnto the knyȝtes of the round table / and al was for to shewe outward that she had as grete Ioye in al other knyghtes of the table round as she had in sir launcelot / al only at that dyner she had sir Gawayne and his bretheren(please add an English translation of this quotation)

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From out- +‎ ward.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, rare) To ward off; to keep out.

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book V, Canto I”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: Ne any armour could his dint out-ward; / But wheresoever it did light, it throughly shard.

definitions.definition: A ward in a detached building connected with a hospital.
